units: a mountain road grows narrower as it climbs
the slope of the ground forces drivers to slow down
cold rain makes the surface dangerous and worsens the delays
the crews in charge of the road spread sand over it
this operation aims to keep heavy vehicles from sliding
traffic runs freely again before night falls
a hamlet set high up is served by no truck
goods are carried up there by pack animals
the people living there approve of this limit, which spares the track
text: The road that climbs toward the pass grows narrower the higher it goes. Its harsh grade forces drivers to ease off, and the slowing traffic backs up into one long line at the first bend. When cold rain sweeps across it, the asphalt turns slick and the line stretches further still. Maintenance crews spread sand on the roadway then, because an iced surface would send the heaviest vehicles sliding. The effect is immediate and plain: traffic settles back into a steady rhythm well before dark. Higher up, a steep track leaves the road and ends at a hamlet no truck ever reaches. With no drivable approach, deliveries come up on the backs of pack animals, which keeps every load small. The people who live there accept the limit, since it spares the track the wear that wheels would grind into it.

units: waiting on an overcrowded platform strongly irritates travelers
transit systems were designed for fewer users
ridership has outgrown capacity without any widening of the lines
buying extra cars is costly and useless if the stops are saturated
the writer proposes spreading ridership over different time slots
he names shifting office hours as one possible measure
he also suggests reserved lanes and cheaper fares outside the rush
places that tried these measures saw peak crowding drop
most riders would agree to leave later in order to sit down
text: Nothing wears a rider's patience thinner than a packed platform with no train in sight. The cause is no mystery. City networks were laid out for a smaller population, and demand has outgrown them while the lines themselves stayed exactly as wide as before. Buying more cars costs a fortune and settles nothing while the stations choke at the very same hour. Another way in deserves a hearing: spread the demand out rather than swallow it whole. Shift the start of the workday, set aside lanes for shared vehicles, cut the fare on quiet runs. Where such steps were tried, the worst of the crush eased with no digging at all. The objection comes back fast, that everyone guards his own timetable. It weakens once you ask the riders, most of whom would trade a later start for a seat.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the driver gladly talks about the start of his working life
his old machine was in poor shape and shut badly
its rattling body warned him of a bend in advance
the vehicle he has now is far more comfortable and quiet
a camera device has taken the place of the old mirror
riders once talked with each other the whole way
today's riders look at their screens in silence
the driver admits the newer equipment is easier on his back
he misses the smell of machinery at start-up, now gone
text: Ask the shuttle driver about his first years behind the wheel and he needs no second invitation. That early machine was worn out: the door never shut properly, the floor buzzed underfoot, and the whole rattling body called out a bend before the turn signal did. What he drives today shares nothing with it. The cab is hushed, the seat backs tilt where you want them, and a camera has taken over from the blind mirror he used to squint into. He measures his riders the same way. Once the entire village boarded together and talked the length of the aisle; now each one stares at a screen, and the run goes by almost without a word. None of that leaves him bitter, he says, because the newer machine is easier on his back. What he misses is the smell of a cold engine at start-up, which nothing built since can give him back.

units: three things catch the eye at the entrance of the renovated building
the entrance area was cramped and poorly lit before the work
glazing now brings daylight all the way down to the steps
the direction signs have been redrawn in large lettering
riders in a hurry find their way without checking a display
the old grimy seats have been taken out of the place
the perches that replaced them are few and uncomfortable
the writer finds the outcome positive on the whole
reaching the platforms no longer calls for a detour
text: Three things catch the eye the moment you step into the rebuilt stop. The first is a matter of volume: the entrance hall, cramped and dim before the work, now opens under a glass roof that carries daylight down to the steps. The second is the signage, redrawn in oversized lettering and plain symbols, so that a rider in a hurry picks out the right track without ever looking up at a display. The third point flatters less. The grubby benches are gone, and what stands in their place is scarce and hard, as though the operator would rather nobody stayed long. The account still comes out ahead. Movement through the hall reads more clearly, reaching the platforms takes no detour anymore, and the hush of the sliding doors is a pleasant shock. One rider put it plainly: you breathe better, you sit less.

units: the person written to had warned of a soaked track after the water rose
the writer set out at first light with his bags strapped down
the first part of the ride was marked by stakes driven into the ground
the ruts left by his wheels closed up right behind him
the rain stopped halfway through the ride
the ground hardened under the wind
a steep climb forced the writer to walk and push his bicycle
he reached a high shelter as evening fell
the keeper of the shelter gave him hot soup
text: You warned me the track would be a swamp once the water had risen, and you were right. I set out at first light, bags strapped down tight, the handlebars heavy as an anchor. The opening stretch, staked out with pale markers, dropped between hedges soaked through, and my wheels cut two clean ruts that the mud swallowed shut behind me. Halfway along, the rain quit and the wind dried the crust of the ground, so I rolled a long easy hour barely thinking about it. Then the climb came, steep and with no end to it, and I got off to push, counting my own steps. As evening fell I reached the shelter on the plateau, hands black, heart light, and the keeper set a bowl of scalding soup down for me. I write to you from the window. The valley is steaming, and I already want to leave again tomorrow.

units: the energy stored by a vehicle grows with the square of its speed
doubling the speed makes the braking distance four times as long
a layer of water slips in between the rubber and the road
that layer cuts the grip and reduces the slowing obtained
the grooves of the tire push the water out to the sides
worn tires can no longer clear that water away
a more heavily loaded vehicle needs more force to slow as much
specialists advise widening the gap between vehicles when these conditions change
text: So what lengthens the stopping distance of a car that is already rolling fast? The first cause is stored energy, which grows with the square of the speed: double the pace and braking takes four times the room. And once the road is wet? A film of water slips in between the rubber and the ground, grip falls away, and the same pressure on the pedal buys less slowing than before. Do the grooves of a tire earn their keep? They throw that film out toward the edges. Worn smooth, they throw nothing out at all, and the car starts to float. And what does the load change? Added mass calls for more force to shed the same speed, so the stop grows longer yet. Engineers pack their whole answer into a single short rule: open up the gap ahead of you as soon as any one of these things changes.

units: a woman traveler reports that her connecting train has been canceled
the clerk blames the disruption on a plant blocking the rails
the incident happened near the mouth of an underground passage
a replacement road vehicle is set to leave from the square
that vehicle will go around the high ground to reach the station she wants
her ticket stays valid at no extra cost
the traveler fears her belongings are too bulky for the center aisle
a luggage hold will take her suitcases
a member of staff will lend a hand stowing the bags
text: At the counter, a traveler reported that her connecting train had just been canceled. The clerk answered that the whole line was affected, since a fallen branch was blocking the rails where they come out of the tunnel. She asked whether anything at all could be arranged before nightfall. He explained that a replacement coach would leave from the square outside and would reach the connecting station by rounding the high ground. The ticket in her hand stayed valid, he added, and nothing further would be charged. She worried about her luggage, too bulky in her view for a crowded center aisle. He put her mind at rest: a hold underneath would take the suitcases, and a member of staff would help load them. She thanked him and made for the exit named on the notice, her relief plain to see.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: carriage by water ruled before wheeled vehicles rose
a boat loaded with grain moved forward with almost no effort
animals hauling the same cargo wore out fast on broken ground
the gap comes from the resistance the ground puts up
overland routes served places the current could not reach
a waterway imposes one direction and one fixed course
the two systems split the work according to the cargo
the boat suited heavy loads carried without haste
the spread of paved roads tipped the balance toward the dry route
text: Long before the wheel took over the long hauls, water carried the greater bulk of everything that moved. A barge loaded with grain slid along the current on almost no effort at all, while a team dragging that same weight over broken ground gave out before half the day was done. The gap lay entirely in resistance: water gives way, mud holds on. Overland routes had one advantage the river could never offer. They went where people wanted them to go, high ground included, whereas the stream laid down its own course and its own direction. So the two networks split the work between them, the boat taking the heavy freight that could wait, the cart taking the short and supple run. Once stone-laid roads began to spread in number, that balance tipped over for good toward the dry route.

units: the writer boils getting a bicycle ready down to three checks
he advises pumping the tires up firm
he recommends looking over the tire surface for cuts
the brake levers must be squeezed while standing still to test the lock
friction parts worn too far have to be replaced
bags hung on the handlebars unbalance the steering
it is better to carry the weight low and toward the back
taking a spare tube and a pump saves you from finishing on foot
text: Getting a bicycle ready for a long ride comes down to three checks, and not a single one more than that. Tires first: pump them up firm, run your thumb along the tread, and hunt for the small cuts where a shard of glass may have lodged. Brakes next: squeeze the levers while standing still, watch whether the wheel locks clean, and swap out any pad whose grooves have worn flat. Then the load: a handlebar hung with bags makes the steering twitchy, so drop the weight low and set it toward the rear wheel. One last piece of advice, plain and obvious as it sounds. Take a spare tube and a pump along, because a flat halfway out turns a fine outing into a long walk home. A quarter of an hour of care in the workshop, and you roll away easy in your mind, with no dread of the first slow rise.

units: the vehicle pulled out after the middle of the night with every seat taken
the engine died at the second pickup point
it came to a stop on the shoulder of a fast road
the driver reported a failure in the fuel system
a woman rider trained in mechanics offered her help
they found a clogged filter and cleared it
the journey started again after a break of about half an hour
the passengers clapped when the engine caught
the company gave the rider a free travel voucher
text: It was past midnight when the coach pulled out of the terminal, packed full, doors hissing, a smell of cold coffee hanging in the aisle. At the second pickup the engine coughed twice and then died flat on the shoulder of the fast road. The driver switched on the hazard lights and announced a fault in the fuel feed. A rider coming home from a course in mechanics offered to help, and between them they traced a clogged filter and cleaned it with a rag and a great deal of patience. The coach pulled away again half an hour later, to clapping from every row. At the far end the operator handed a free travel voucher to the woman who had bailed out its driver. She said what she had really wanted was her own bed, and that the breakdown had woken her for nothing. The rest walked off already telling the story into their phones.
